translationRepairs: Yelü Chucai, whose courtesy name was Jinqing, was a great-great-grandson in the eighth generation of Yelü Tuyu, the Liao Prince of Dongdan.
Yelü Chucai, whose courtesy name was Jinqing, was an eighth-generation descendant of Yelü Tuyu, the Liao Prince of Dongdan.
八世孫 means an eighth-generation descendant; 'great-great-grandson in the eighth generation' wrongly conflates degrees of descent with generation count.

Xiandebo, nursing an old grudge, hated him all the more and slandered him to a imperial prince: "The Yelü director of the Secretariat fills his office with kin and cronies; he must be disloyal—memorialize for his execution."

Xiandebo, nursing an old grudge, hated him all the more and slandered him to an imperial prince: "The Yelü director of the Secretariat fills his office with kin and cronies; he must be disloyal—memorialize for his execution."
'a imperial prince' is ungrammatical; English requires 'an' before the vowel onset of imperial.

Thereupon he memorialized to establish tax-collection commissioners for the ten circuits including Yanjing; all chief and deputy posts were filled with scholar-officials such as Chen Shike and Zhao Fang, all men of generous and mature character, the finest selection in the realm, and assistants were all drawn from former personnel of the provincial departments.

Thereupon he memorialized to establish tax-collection commissioners for the ten circuits including Yanjing; all chief and deputy posts were filled with scholar-officials such as Chen Shike and Zhao Fang, all men of generous and mature character, the finest selection in the realm, and assistants were all drawn from former personnel of the Secretariat and ministries.
省部 means the central Secretariat and ministries, not provincial departments; the proposed correction matches the Chinese and the idiomatic field.

He ordered Liu Zhong, tax commissioner of Xuanede, to hold examinations in every commandery in three fields—classics, rhapsodies, and policy essays. Captured scholars enslaved were also to sit the exam; masters who hid them were put to death.

He ordered Liu Zhong, tax commissioner of Xuande, to hold examinations in every commandery in three fields—classics, rhapsodies, and policy essays. Captured scholars enslaved were also to sit the exam; masters who hid them were put to death.
宣德州 is Xuande Prefecture; 'Xuanede' is a misspelling of the place-name.

Thereupon he ordered Liu Zhong, tax commissioner of Xuanede Prefecture, to conduct examinations in each commandery, divided into three categories—classics, rhapsodies, and discourses; Confucian scholars taken captive as slaves were also ordered to sit the examination, and masters who concealed them and did not send them were to die.

Thereupon he ordered Liu Zhong, tax commissioner of Xuande Prefecture, to conduct examinations in each commandery, divided into three categories—classics, rhapsodies, and discourses; Confucian scholars taken captive as slaves were also ordered to sit the examination, and masters who concealed them and did not send them were to die.
Same place-name error in the literal field: 宣德州 is Xuande Prefecture, not Xuanede.
He answered, "Even a father teaching his sons does not wish them to fall into wickedness.
He answered, "A ruler or father, in instructing his ministers or sons, likewise would not wish them to fall into unrighteousness.
君父教臣子 pairs ruler/father with ministers/sons. The revision restores the political and familial parallel without the awkward suggestion that one person is simultaneously both lord and father.
The palace favorite again accused Chucai of violating regulations; the Emperor was angry and imprisoned Chucai;
The palace favorite again accused Chucai of violating regulations; the Emperor was angry and had Chucai bound;
系楚材 means he was bound/fettered; the next unit 不肯解縛 confirms binding, so 'imprisoned' overstates the Chinese.

The emperor loved wine and drank daily with his ministers; Chucai remonstrated repeatedly in vain, then brought a wine trough with an iron spout and said, "Ferment can rot iron—what will it do to the five organs!"

The emperor loved wine and drank daily with his ministers; Chucai remonstrated repeatedly in vain, then brought a wine trough with an iron spout and said, "Ferment can corrode things; if even iron is like this, how much more the five organs!"
曲蘗能腐物，鐵尚如此，況五臟乎 is an a fortiori from the corroded iron to the viscera. 'Ferment' is more historically precise than 'yeast,' and the revision preserves the argument's progression.
The emperor reproached Chucai: "You said Confucian teaching could govern the realm and that scholars were good men—why then do we have men like these?"
The emperor reproached Chucai: "You said Confucius's teaching could govern the realm and that Confucians are good men—why then do we have men like these?"
孔子之教 names Confucius, and 儒者 are Confucians; 'Confucian teaching'/'scholars' erases the named 孔子 and the class noun in the Chinese.

In the first year of Zhishun he was posthumously given the title Merit-holder Who Deliberates on State Regulation with Vigorous Brilliance and Assists the Mandate, Grand Preceptor, and Upper Pillar of the State, enfeoffed posthumously as Prince of Guangning, with the temple name Wenzheng.

In the first year of Zhishun he was posthumously given the title Merit-holder Who Deliberates on State Regulation with Vigorous Brilliance and Assists the Mandate, Grand Preceptor, and Upper Pillar of the State, enfeoffed posthumously as Prince of Guangning, with the posthumous name Wenzheng.
諡文正 is a posthumous name (諡號), not a temple name (廟號).
In the first year of Zhishun he was posthumously honored as Grand Preceptor and Upper Pillar of the State, enfeoffed as Prince of Guangning, with the posthumous name Wenzheng.

In the first year of Zhishun he was posthumously honored as Merit-holder Who Deliberates on State Regulation with Vigorous Brilliance and Assists the Mandate, Grand Preceptor, and Upper Pillar of the State, enfeoffed as Prince of Guangning, with the posthumous name Wenzheng.
The idiomatic omits the conferred merit title 經國議制寅亮佐運功臣 that the Chinese grants alongside the other honors.
His sons were Xian and Zhu.
His sons were Xuan and Zhu.
鉉 is Xuàn; English 'Xian' is the wrong reading of the given name.
His sons were Xian and Zhu.
His sons were Xuan and Zhu.
The literal field has the same wrong reading: 鉉 is Xuan, not Xian.

In the first year of Zhishun he was posthumously given the title Merit-holder Who Promotes Loyalty, Preserves Virtue, and Expands Strength in Assisting Governance, Grand Preceptor, Grand Master with Honor Equal to the Three Excellencies, Upper Pillar of the State, Prince of Yining, with the temple name Wenzhong.

In the first year of Zhishun he was posthumously given the title Merit-holder Who Promotes Loyalty, Preserves Virtue, and Expands Strength in Assisting Governance, Grand Preceptor, Grand Master with Honor Equal to the Three Excellencies, Upper Pillar of the State, Prince of Yining, with the posthumous name Wenzhong.
諡文忠 is a posthumous name, not a temple name.

In the first year of Zhishun he was posthumously honored as Grand Preceptor, Grand Master with Honor Equal to the Three Excellencies, Upper Pillar of the State, and Prince of Yining, with the posthumous name Wenzhong.

In the first year of Zhishun he was posthumously honored as Merit-holder Who Promotes Loyalty, Preserves Virtue, and Expands Strength in Assisting Governance, Grand Preceptor, Grand Master with Honor Equal to the Three Excellencies, Upper Pillar of the State, and Prince of Yining, with the posthumous name Wenzhong.
The idiomatic omits the conferred merit title 推忠保德宣力佐治功臣 present in the Chinese.
He died and was posthumously made Grand Commandant, enfeoffed as Duke of Wei, with the temple name Zhongwu.
He died and was posthumously made Grand Commandant, enfeoffed as Duke of Wei, with the posthumous name Zhongwu.
諡忠武 is a posthumous name, not a temple name.

At the time the various army commanders were overbearing and extravagant, harming the people; the thousand-household chief Guo was especially so, killing a man's husband and seizing his wife; Weizhong executed him as a warning, and Guanzhong was solemnly ordered.

At the time the various army commanders were overbearing and extravagant, harming the people; the thousand-household chief Guo was especially so, killing a man and seizing his wife; Weizhong executed him as a warning, and Guanzhong was solemnly ordered.
殺人之夫而奪其妻 means killing a (woman's) husband and seizing his wife; 'a man's husband' is a mistranslation.

At the time the various army commanders were overbearing and extravagant, harming the people; the thousand-household chief Guo was especially so, killing a man and seizing his wife; Weizhong executed him as a warning, and Guanzhong was solemnly ordered.

At the time the various army commanders were overbearing and extravagant, harming the people; the thousand-household chief Guo was especially so, killing a man and seizing his wife; Weizhong executed him as a warning, and Guanzhong was awed into order.
關中肅然 means that Guanzhong was awed and brought to order; 'solemnly ordered' is not grammatical English and misconstrues 肅然.
In the second year of Zhongtong he was posthumously given the temple name Duke Zhongsu.
In the second year of Zhongtong he was posthumously given the title Duke Zhongsu.
追諡曰忠肅公 grants a posthumous title, not a temple name. The revision avoids the awkward phrase 'posthumous name Duke Zhongsu.'

Earlier, when Kublai campaigned against Song at Bian, Nanhe said, "Li Tan has received great favor from the state and holds a region on his own, yet his followers are treacherous—rebellion is only a matter of time."

Earlier, when Kublai campaigned against Song at Bian, Nanhe said, "Li Tan has received great favor from the state and holds a region on his own, yet he is deeply deceitful—rebellion is only a matter of time."
其人多詐 predicates deceit of Li Tan himself, not of his followers. The revision states that naturally rather than using the stilted phrase 'the man is full of deceit.'

Earlier, when Shizu campaigned against Song at Bian, Nanhe advanced and said, "Li Tan has received deep favor from the state and controls a region on his own, yet his people are full of deceit—rebellion is only a matter of time."

Earlier, when Shizu campaigned against Song at Bian, Nanhe advanced and said, "Li Tan has received deep favor from the state and controls a region on his own, yet he is full of deceit—rebellion is only a matter of time."
其人多詐 describes Li Tan himself as deceitful; it does not refer to his people.
